title: Data Product Management
summary: Product management where the product is data: datasets, metrics layers, data platforms and the trust people place in the numbers.
tests: Whether you can treat data as a product with users and quality bars, govern it responsibly, and choose between many teams' requests.

rounds.title: Data Product Sense
rounds.focus: Who uses the data, for what decision, and what product serves them.

rounds.title: Data Quality and Trust
rounds.focus: Making numbers people can rely on.

rounds.title: Governance and Privacy
rounds.focus: Access, purpose and personal data — designed in, not added later.

rounds.title: Prioritisation Across Teams
rounds.focus: Choosing between many teams' data requests.

rounds.title: Behavioural
rounds.focus: Ownership when the numbers are wrong.

questions.title: One definition of 'active customer'
questions.prompt: Five teams in your company report five different numbers for 'active customers'. You are asked to build a shared metrics layer. How do you approach it as a product?
hints: Who uses these numbers, and for which decisions?
Why do the definitions differ — mistakes or genuinely different needs?
How will teams adopt the shared definition?
followups: Finance refuses to change its definition because it is in investor reports. What now?
How do you measure the success of the metrics layer?
Who owns a definition once it exists?
criteria: Interviews consumers and finds the decisions behind each number.
Distinguishes legitimate variants from errors; names them distinctly.
Defines the product: governed definitions, an interface, documentation, owners.
Plans adoption and deprecation of old numbers.
Measures trust and adoption.
outline: Discovery: each team's definition, decision, audience.
Reconcile: one canonical metric plus named variants (e.g. 'billing-active', 'product-active').
Product: definitions as code; shared semantic layer; documentation; owner per metric; change process.
Adoption: migrate top dashboards first; label legacy numbers.
Success: share of key dashboards on the layer; reconciliation incidents; time to answer metric questions.
questions.reference:
I would treat it as a product with users. First, discovery: for each of the five numbers, who uses it, for which decision and why it is defined that way. Some differences are mistakes; others reflect real needs — Finance may count paying customers, Product people who used the app.

The answer is rarely one number. It is one canonical definition plus clearly named variants — ‘paying customers’, ‘product-active users’ — each with an owner, written as code in a shared semantic layer and documented where people look. A change process means definitions do not move silently.

Adoption: migrate the most-viewed dashboards first, label legacy numbers as such, and retire them on a schedule. Finance can keep its investor-reporting definition as a named variant; what matters is that nobody confuses it with product activity.

Success: share of important dashboards built on the layer, fewer ‘why don’t these match?’ incidents, and time to answer a metric question.

questions.title: Selling data to customers
questions.prompt: Your logistics company wants to sell delivery-performance data to its business customers as a paid analytics product. What would you build first, and what would you not do?
hints: Which customer decisions would this data improve?
Whose data is it, and what are you allowed to share?
What does a minimum useful product look like?
followups: A customer wants to see how competitors' deliveries perform. Can you show it?
How do you prevent the numbers from being wrong in a customer's board meeting?
criteria: Starts from customer decisions.
Respects data ownership and confidentiality between customers.
Defines an MVP with reliable core metrics.
Sets quality SLAs for external numbers.
Plans pricing and validation with design partners.
outline: Customer jobs: carrier selection, promise dates, complaint reduction.
Data rights: only each customer's own data; aggregated benchmarks only with thresholds that prevent identification.
MVP: on-time rate, delay causes, regional heatmap; exports.
Quality: freshness SLA, reconciliation, change log.
Validate with design partners; price by tier.
questions.reference:
I would start with the decisions customers make: which delivery options to promise, where delays hurt them, and when to complain or switch. The first product is their own delivery performance — on-time rate, delay causes, regional patterns — delivered reliably, with exports.

What I would not do: show one customer’s data to another. Benchmarks can come later, only aggregated across enough customers that no single one can be identified, and only if contracts allow it.

External numbers must be right, so the product has freshness commitments, reconciliation with operational systems and a public change log when definitions change. I would build with three to five design partners who agree to pay if it helps, and price in tiers by depth of analysis.

questions.title: The dashboard was wrong for a week
questions.prompt: The revenue dashboard executives use every morning showed wrong numbers for a week because an upstream team renamed a field. Nobody noticed until a sales leader questioned it. What do you change?
hints: Why did nobody notice for a week?
How could the upstream team have known their change would break you?
What do consumers need to see when data is wrong?
followups: The upstream team says they cannot check every consumer. Respond.
How do you rebuild executives' trust?
Which checks would you add first?
criteria: Handles the immediate issue: correct, communicate, mark affected period.
Introduces data contracts at the producer boundary.
Adds monitoring: freshness, volume, schema and value checks with alerts.
Shows data status to consumers.
Defines ownership and incident process for data.
outline: Immediate: fix, backfill, annotate the affected week, tell executives clearly.
Contracts: producers declare schema and semantics; breaking changes need notice; checks in their CI.
Monitoring: schema change detection; anomaly checks on key metrics; freshness.
Visibility: data status banner on dashboards.
Process: data incidents treated like production incidents with reviews.
questions.reference:
Immediately: fix the pipeline, recompute the affected week, mark the period on the dashboard and tell executives plainly what was wrong and what decisions might have been affected.

The root problem is that a producer could break a critical consumer without knowing. I would introduce data contracts for critical sources: the producer declares the fields and their meaning, and a breaking change fails a check in the producer’s own build pipeline unless coordinated. The upstream team does not need to know every consumer; the contract tells them.

Then detection: alerts on schema changes, freshness and unusual values for key metrics, so a wrong number is caught in hours, not by a sales leader. Dashboards show a data-status indicator when checks fail. Finally, data incidents get the same process as production incidents: an owner, a timeline and a review. Trust comes back through visible reliability over several weeks.

questions.title: Access to customer data for analysts
questions.prompt: Analysts currently get broad access to raw customer data, including personal information, with a ticket. Leadership wants faster analysis and better privacy. Design the access product.
hints: Do analysts usually need names and emails?
What does purpose-based access mean in practice?
How do you keep the compliant path faster than a workaround?
followups: A data scientist needs raw data to debug a model. How do they get it?
criteria: Classifies data by sensitivity.
Gives most users de-identified data by default.
Grants sensitive access by purpose, time-limited, approved and audited.
Makes the compliant path self-service and fast.
Handles retention and deletion.
outline: Classify: public, internal, personal, sensitive.
Default: de-identified, aggregated datasets self-service.
Elevated: request with purpose; time-limited; approved by data owner; logged.
Tooling: catalog showing sensitivity; masking in query engine.
Audit: regular review of access and use.
Deletion: requests propagate to derived datasets.
questions.reference:
Most analysis does not need names, emails or exact addresses. So the default product is a self-service catalog of de-identified datasets — identifiers replaced, sensitive fields masked — which covers most questions with no ticket at all. That is both faster and more private.

For work that genuinely needs personal data, access is by purpose: the analyst states why, the data owner approves, access expires automatically, and every query is logged. Masking is enforced in the query engine, not by convention.

I would publish sensitivity labels in the catalog, review access regularly, and make sure deletion requests reach derived tables and extracts. The measure of success: time to access for common analysis falls, while the number of people with standing access to raw personal data drops sharply.
pitfalls: Governance as a slower ticket queue.

questions.title: Twelve teams, one data team
questions.prompt: Twelve teams send requests to your data platform team: new tables, dashboards, data feeds. The backlog is three months long and everyone is unhappy. What do you do?
hints: Which requests are one-offs and which repeat?
How do teams see what is being prioritised and why?
What could teams do themselves with the right tools?
followups: The CEO's chief of staff wants their request first. How do you handle it?
How do you measure whether the change worked?
criteria: Analyses requests to find patterns.
Moves recurring needs into self-service capabilities.
Creates a transparent prioritisation forum and criteria.
Says no with reasons and alternatives.
Measures lead time and satisfaction.
outline: Analyse the backlog: categories, repeats, value.
Platform: self-service for common requests (templates, governed datasets).
Intake: one form with decision and value; shared priority review monthly.
Criteria: business value, number of teams helped, effort.
Communicate decisions; publish roadmap.
Metrics: lead time, share self-served, satisfaction.
questions.reference:
I would analyse the backlog first. Usually a large share of requests repeat in different forms — ‘a table of X by week’, ‘a dashboard for Y’. Those become product capabilities: governed core datasets and templates teams can use themselves, so they no longer need us.

For the rest, a single intake asks what decision the request supports and its value. A monthly review with representatives of the main teams sets priorities against published criteria: value, number of teams helped, effort. Decisions and the roadmap are visible, including what we declined and the alternative offered.

Requests from senior people go through the same process, with their value stated; urgent ones can jump the queue if the criteria support it. Success: lead time for requests, share of needs met by self-service, and requester satisfaction.

questions.title: When your numbers were wrong
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time data you were responsible for was wrong and someone made a decision on it.
hints: What did you tell the decision-maker?
followups: What check would have caught it?
criteria: Owns the error.
Communicated quickly and clearly.
Helped repair the decision.
Fixed the root cause.
Specific lesson.
outline: Situation and the decision made.
How the error was found.
Communication.
Repair.
Root-cause fix.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “A marketing team cut spend on a channel because our attribution table showed poor returns. Two weeks later I found that a join was dropping mobile conversions for that channel. I told the marketing lead the same day, with corrected numbers and the size of the error. They restored part of the budget. We added a reconciliation check against total conversions and now publish known limitations next to each attribution report.”
